explanation: The seller obligates himself to transfer ownership and deliver a determinate thing; the buyer pays a price certain in money or its equivalent. The sale may be absolute or conditional.

A sale is consensual: agreement on the thing and price ordinarily perfects it. Delivery, payment, notarization, or registration generally go to performance, proof, enforceability, or third-party effect — not to perfection itself.
Consent is manifested by the meeting of offer and acceptance on the object and cause. The offer must be certain and the acceptance absolute; a qualified acceptance is a counteroffer.

An option contract is a separate preparatory contract keeping an offer open for a period; it requires consideration distinct from the price to bind the offeror. A unilateral promise without distinct consideration may be withdrawn before acceptance is communicated — but while unwithdrawn it can operate as an offer, and timely acceptance before communicated withdrawal can produce a binding sale.

The Statute of Frauds requires a sufficient written memorandum for certain executory agreements — including specified sales of goods and interests in real property — to be enforceable by action. Partial performance or failure to timely object to oral evidence can take a case outside the bar. It does not make every oral land sale void.

Emptio rei speratae: sale of an expected thing; efficacy depends on the thing coming into existence. Emptio spei: purchase of the hope or chance itself; the buyer may bear the risk even if the expected thing never materializes, if that is what the parties truly contracted for.
If the consideration is primarily another thing, analyze barter; if money predominates, sale rules generally govern. Compare values where both money and thing are involved.
The parties may expressly reserve ownership until full payment or another condition. Analyze the actual clause.

Ownership ordinarily transfers upon actual or legally recognized constructive delivery — including execution of a public instrument (Art. 1498), traditio longa manu, traditio brevi manu, and constitutum possessorium (Art. 1500) — not at the bare moment of perfection.

Sale on return: the buyer may return the goods; title and risk generally remain with the seller until approval or expiry of the return period. Sale on approval, trial, or satisfaction: title generally passes on signified approval, adoption of the transaction, or retention beyond the stated or reasonable time without rejection.

The buyer may suspend payment where disturbed in possession or ownership, or with well-founded fear of disturbance — subject to the statutory exception and the seller's provision of security. It is a defense under prescribed conditions, not a general license to stop paying.

Double sale of the same thing to different buyers: movables go to the buyer who first takes possession in good faith; immovables to the buyer who in good faith first records in the Registry (absent inscription, first in possession in good faith; absent both, the oldest title in good faith). Applies only where the same seller made two or more valid sales of exactly the same property.

Art. 1545 addresses conditions and their relation to breach. Art. 1546 covers express warranties: an affirmation of fact or promise relating to the thing can be a warranty if it naturally tends to induce purchase and the buyer relies on it. Mere opinion or dealer's talk is generally not a warranty (Arts. 1341, 1546) unless the statutory facts — such as expert status and reliance — apply.

Implied warranty of title and eviction. Eviction (Art. 1548) occurs when, by final judgment based on a right prior to the sale or an act imputable to the seller, the buyer is deprived of all or part of the thing — learned as a five-element checklist, with remedies under Arts. 1555–1556.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Implied warranty of title and eviction

explanation: Hidden defects (Arts. 1561–1571) and non-apparent burdens on immovables (Art. 1560). Remedies: accion redhibitoria (withdraw from/rescind the sale; the thing is returned and price/expenses are handled under the Code) or accion quanti minoris (buyer keeps the thing but seeks a proportional reduction of price). Arts. 1568–1569 address loss of the thing because of the hidden defect or a fortuitous event and the seller's knowledge; the seller's knowledge can affect damages.
Six-month period for actions for hidden defects, counted from delivery. Special laws and contractual warranties can alter the analysis — do not assume every warranty claim shares this period.

Risk is generally allocated by reference to whether property in the goods has passed, unless the parties agree otherwise — but special rules govern seller/buyer fault, delay, shipment, sales on return or approval, hidden defects, and fungible goods priced by weight, number, or measure.

For sales of personal property payable in installments, Art. 1484 gives the seller an election: (1) exact fulfillment; (2) cancellation after failure to pay two or more installments; or (3) foreclosure of the chattel mortgage if constituted. Choosing foreclosure bars any deficiency recovery. Art. 1485 extends the rules to covered lease-with-option structures; Art. 1486 limits retention stipulations.

Protects buyers of residential real estate on installment payments. At least two years of installments (Sec. 3): grace of one month per year of payments, cancellation only after 30-day notarial notice with cash surrender value (50% of payments, plus 5% per year beyond five, capped at 90%). Below two years (Sec. 4): at least 60 days' grace plus the 30-day notice requirement. Verify coverage and read the statute directly for thresholds and computation.

Condominium sales: keep distinct the buyer's right to suspend installments on developer failure (Sec. 23) from the developer's rights when the buyer defaults without just cause (Sec. 24), plus the Sec. 25 title-delivery rule. Review covered project/developer definitions in the actual law.

Conventional redemption: the seller reserves the right to repurchase (Art. 1601), with period rules under Art. 1606 including a statutory default and maximum. Art. 1602 lists circumstances presuming an equitable mortgage; Art. 1603 construes doubtful pacto de retro contracts as equitable mortgages. Art. 2088 prohibits pactum commissorium.

Legal redemption by operation of law: co-owners (Art. 1620), co-heirs under Art. 1088, and adjoining rural/urban owners (Arts. 1621–1622), with notice and period rules under Art. 1623. Identify the class, triggering sale/notice, and start date before giving a deadline.

citation: RA 9160, Sec. 2, as amended by RA 11521
explanation: State policy to protect the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts, keep the Philippines from being used as a money-laundering site, cooperate in transnational investigations/prosecutions, and implement targeted financial sanctions. Banking privacy and AMLA enforcement work together: privacy is not absolute when a lawful AMLA process applies.
verbatim: It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect and preserve the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts and to ensure that the Philippines shall not be used as a money laundering site for the proceeds of any unlawful activity. Consistent with its foreign policy, the State shall extend cooperation in transnational investigations and prosecutions of persons involved in money laundering activities wherever committed, as well as in the implementation of targeted financial sanctions related to the financing of the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, and financing of terrorism, pursuant to the resolution of the United Nations Security Council.

citation: RA 10365, Sec. 1 (amending AMLA Sec. 3(a)), read with RA 11521
explanation: Defines covered persons across BSP-, IC-, and SEC-supervised sectors plus designated businesses (jewelry, company service providers, client-asset managers). RA 11521 adds real estate developers/brokers and offshore gaming operators/service providers. Covered persons bear customer-identification, record-keeping, monitoring, and reporting duties.
verbatim: ‘Covered persons’, natural or juridical, refer to: (1) banks, non-banks, quasi-banks, trust entities, foreign exchange dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance and transfer companies and other similar entities and all other persons and their subsidiaries and affiliates supervised or regulated by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP); (2) insurance companies, pre-need companies and all other persons supervised or regulated by the Insurance Commission (IC); (3) (i) securities dealers, brokers, salesmen, investment houses and other similar persons managing securities or rendering services as investment agent, advisor, or consultant, (ii) mutual funds, close-end investment companies, common trust funds, and other similar persons, and (iii) other entities administering or otherwise dealing in currency, commodities or financial derivatives based thereon, valuable objects, cash substitutes and other similar monetary instruments or property supervised or regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC); (4) jewelry dealers in precious metals, who, as a business, trade in precious metals, for transactions in excess of One million pesos (₱1,000,000.00); (5) jewelry dealers in precious stones, who, as a business, trade in precious stones, for transactions in excess of One million pesos (₱1,000,000.00); (6) company service providers which, as a business, provide services to third parties such as acting as a formation agent, director or corporate secretary, providing a registered office or business address, or acting as a nominee shareholder; and (7) persons who provide services such as managing client money, securities or other assets; managing bank, savings or securities accounts; organizing contributions for companies; or creating, operating or managing juridical persons or arrangements and buying or selling business entities.

explanation: Customer-identification duty: establish/record true identity on official documents, verify corporate clients' existence/structure/representatives, and never open anonymous or fictitious-name accounts (non-checking numbered accounts allowed). Restated by 2018 IRR Rule 18, Sec. 3.1 for all customers, agents, and legal arrangements.
verbatim: (a) Customer Identification. — Covered persons shall establish and record the true identity of their clients based on official documents. They shall maintain a system of verifying the true identity of their clients and, in case of corporate clients, require a system of verifying their legal existence and organizational structure, as well as the authority and identification of all persons purporting to act on their behalf. Anonymous accounts, accounts under fictitious names, and all other similar accounts shall be absolutely prohibited, subject to the statutory allowance for non-checking numbered accounts.

explanation: Record-keeping duty: keep all transaction records for 5 years from the transaction; for closed accounts, keep identification, account files, and correspondence for at least 5 years from closure, so fund movements can be reconstructed.
verbatim: All records of all transactions of covered persons shall be maintained and safely stored for five (5) years from the date of transactions. With respect to closed accounts, the records on customer identification, account files and business correspondence shall be preserved and safely stored for at least five (5) years from the dates when they were closed.

explanation: Reporting duty: report all covered and suspicious transactions within 5 working days (supervising authority may allow up to 10); dual-nature transactions are reported as suspicious. Good-faith reporters are immune from proceedings; covered persons/officers/employees must not tip off customers. The Sec. 9(c) confidentiality rule binds covered persons, not AMLC's own investigative disclosures (Republic v. Sandiganbayan).
verbatim:
Covered persons shall report to the AMLC all covered transactions and suspicious transactions within five (5) working days from occurrence thereof, unless the Supervising Authority prescribes a longer period not exceeding ten (10) working days. Should a transaction be determined to be both a covered transaction and a suspicious transaction, the covered person shall be required to report the same as a suspicious transaction.

However, no administrative, criminal or civil proceedings shall lie against any person for having made a covered or suspicious transaction report in the regular performance of his duties in good faith, whether or not such reporting results in any criminal prosecution under this Act or any other law.

explanation: Threshold-based reporting trigger: general cash/equivalent over ₱500,000 in one banking day; single casino cash over ₱5,000,000; single real-estate cash over ₱7,500,000; the IRR adds jewelry/precious-metal/stone dealer transactions over ₱1,000,000. Crossing the threshold triggers reporting, not criminal liability. The old ₱4M/five-days threshold is obsolete.
verbatim: ‘Covered transactions’ is a transaction in cash or other equivalent monetary instrument involving a total amount in excess of Five hundred thousand pesos (₱500,000.00) within one (1) banking day; for covered persons under Section 3(a)(8), a single casino cash transaction involving an amount in excess of Five million pesos (₱5,000,000.00) or its equivalent in any other currency. For covered persons under Section 3(a)(9) herein, a single cash transaction involving an amount in excess of Seven million five hundred thousand pesos (₱7,500,000.00) or its equivalent in any other currency.

explanation: Monetary instrument covers currency and financial instruments (coins/currency, drafts, checks, notes, securities and similar instruments through which title can pass). Person means any natural or juridical person. Proceeds means an amount derived or realized from an unlawful activity. Transaction means any act establishing a right/obligation or contractual/legal relationship, including any movement of funds by any means with a covered institution. (Reviewer presents these defined terms with gloss rather than a single continuous quotation; no verbatim field.)

Seven red flags with no minimum amount: no legal/trade purpose; unidentified client; amount incommensurate with capacity; structuring to evade reporting; deviation from client profile; link to unlawful activity; or similar/analogous transactions. An STR is financial intelligence for analysis, not proof of guilt.
verbatim: ‘Suspicious transactions’ are transactions with covered persons, regardless of the amounts involved, where any of the following circumstances exist: (1) There is no underlying legal or trade obligation, purpose or economic justification; (2) The client is not properly identified; (3) The amount involved is not commensurate with the business or financial capacity of the client; (4) Taking into account all known circumstances, it may be perceived that the client’s transaction is structured in order to avoid being the subject of reporting requirements under the Act; (5) Any circumstance relating to the transaction which is observed to deviate from the profile of the client and/or the client’s past transactions with the covered person; (6) The transaction is in any way related to an unlawful activity or offense under this Act that is about to be, is being or has been committed; or (7) Any transaction that is similar or analogous to any of the foregoing.

citation: 2018 AMLA IRR, Rule 2 and Rule 23 (Jan. 2021 amendment)
explanation: Beneficial owner = the natural person who ultimately owns/controls the customer or on whose behalf the transaction is done. The SEC builds the identification/record-keeping/publication mechanisms, requires accurate and regularly updated beneficial-ownership information, and ensures juridical persons cooperate with AMLC/supervising authorities, including through an authorized resident natural person.

sourceRefs.section: 5. Beneficial ownership (2018 AMLA IRR, Rules 23 and 24)

verbatim:
‘Beneficial Owner’ refers to any natural person who: (1) ultimately owns or controls the customer and/or on whose behalf a transaction or activity is being conducted.

The SEC is hereby enlisted to develop mechanisms that identify and describe the following: (a) Different types, forms and basic features of legal persons in the country; (b) Processes for the creation of those legal persons; and (c) Processes for obtaining and recording of basic and beneficial ownership information. The SEC shall develop a mechanism to make the information on the legal persons and their beneficial owners publicly available, as may be allowed under existing laws.

The SEC shall require companies and corporate clients, respectively, to submit accurate and regularly updated beneficial ownership information.

explanation: For legal arrangements, covered persons must require express-trust trustees to obtain and hold adequate, accurate, current identity information on trustors/grantors/settlors, the trustee, beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and any other natural person exercising ultimate effective control. (Only the quoted phrase below is an explicit quotation; the balance is the reviewer's paraphrase.)

sourceRefs.section: 5. Beneficial ownership (2018 AMLA IRR, Rules 23 and 24)

verbatim: adequate, accurate, and current information

explanation: Accounts only in the true and full name of the owner/holder; anonymous/fictitious/similar accounts absolutely prohibited; only non-checking numbered accounts allowed, and their CTRs/STRs must name the true holder; supervising authorities may test annually for such accounts. (Syllabus cites Rule 2, Sec. 1(1)(n), but that is the 'Beneficiary' definition in the amended IRR; Rule 17 is the operative rule.)
verbatim:
Section 1. Anonymous Accounts and Accounts under Fictitious Names. 1.1. Covered persons shall maintain customers’ account only in the true and full name of the account owner or holder. 1.2. Anonymous accounts, accounts under fictitious names, and all other similar accounts shall be absolutely prohibited.

Section 2. Numbered Accounts. 2.1. Numbered accounts, except non-checking numbered accounts, shall not be allowed. 2.2. CTRs and STRs involving non-checking numbered accounts shall contain the true name of the account holder.

Section 3. Annual Testing to Determine True Identity of Accounts. The SAs may conduct annual testing for the sole purpose of determining the existence and true identity of the foregoing accounts, if any.

explanation: CDD purposes (identify customer/agents/beneficial owners; assess risk; manage the relationship; calibrate monitoring), six CDD measures (identification, verification, agent checks, beneficial-ownership verification, purpose determination, ongoing monitoring), scrutiny of complex/unusual transactions with EDD for higher risk, and refusal/termination plus STR filing when CDD cannot be completed.
verbatim:
Covered persons shall conduct CDD for the following purposes: (a) To identify the customer, and its agents and beneficial owners; (b) To determine the risk posed by each customer; (c) To establish, maintain, close or terminate the account or business relationship; and (d) To assess the level of monitoring to be applied.

Covered persons shall conduct the appropriate CDD measures, which include the following procedures: (a) Customer Identification Process; (b) Customer Verification Process; (c) Identification and Verification of Agents; (d) Beneficial Ownership Verification; (e) Determination of the Purpose of Relationship; and (f) Ongoing Monitoring Process.

Covered persons shall identify and record the true identity of their customers, whether permanent or occasional, and whether natural or juridical person, or legal arrangement.

Covered persons shall examine the background and purpose of all complex, unusually large transactions, all unusual patterns of transactions, which have no apparent economic or lawful purpose, and other transactions that may be considered suspicious. Where the risks are higher, covered persons shall conduct EDD.

explanation: Six modes of committing money laundering with knowledge that the instrument/property represents, involves, or relates to proceeds of unlawful activity: transact; convert/transfer/dispose/move/acquire/possess/use; conceal/disguise; attempt/conspire; aid/abet/assist/counsel; or facilitate by act or omission. Knowledge and the proceeds link must be established.
verbatim: Money laundering is committed by any person who, knowing that any monetary instrument or property represents, involves, or relates to the proceeds of any unlawful activity: (a) transacts said monetary instrument or property; (b) converts, transfers, disposes of, moves, acquires, possesses or uses said monetary instrument or property; (c) conceals or disguises the true nature, source, location, disposition, movement or ownership of or rights with respect to said monetary instrument or property; (d) attempts or conspires to commit money laundering offenses referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c); (e) aids, abets, assists in or counsels the commission of the money laundering offenses referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) above; and (f) performs or fails to perform any act as a result of which he facilitates the offense of money laundering referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) above.

explanation: Lists predicate/unlawful activities whose proceeds may be laundered: kidnapping for ransom; drugs; graft/plunder; robbery/extortion; illegal gambling; piracy; qualified theft; swindling; smuggling; e-commerce/securities offenses; hijacking; terrorism/terrorism financing; bribery/corruption; public-funds frauds; forgery/counterfeiting; trafficking; forestry/fisheries/mining/wildlife/caves offenses; carnapping; illegal firearms/explosives; fencing; migrant-worker offenses; IP offenses; voyeurism; child-protection offenses; strategic-trade/WMD-proliferation-financing violations; and specified tax crimes. Use the full current Sec. 3(i) text; list and numbering have been amended. (No verbatim: reviewer summarizes categories.)

AMLC = BSP Governor (chair) + IC Commissioner + SEC Chairman, acting unanimously. Functions: investigate suspicious/covered-deemed-suspicious transactions; institute forfeiture/remedial proceedings via OSG; cause prosecution complaints; investigate money laundering; seek search/seizure orders and subpoenas; implement targeted financial sanctions; manage frozen/forfeited assets.
verbatim: The Anti-Money Laundering Council is hereby created and shall be composed of the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas as Chairman, the Commissioner of the Insurance Commission and the Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, as members. The AMLC shall act unanimously in the discharge of its functions.

explanation: CA-issued freeze order on AMLC's verified ex parte petition upon probable cause: effective immediately for 20 days, summary hearing with notice, total cap 6 months. RTC asset-preservation orders in proper proceedings; deemed lifted if no case filed in time (pending-case rules apply); limited to the probable-cause amount; the account holder may move to lift. Ongpin: AMLC bears the burden of proving probable cause with a specific account-to-activity link.

sourceRefs.section: 8(a). Freezing of monetary instrument or property (Section 10)

verbatim: Upon a verified ex parte petition by the AMLC and after determination that probable cause exists that any monetary instrument or property is in any way related to an unlawful activity as defined in Section 3(i) hereof, the Court of Appeals may issue a freeze order which shall be effective immediately, for a period of twenty (20) days. Within the twenty (20)-day period, the Court of Appeals shall conduct a summary hearing, with notice to the parties, to determine whether or not to modify or lift the freeze order, or extend its effectivity. The total period of the freeze order issued by the Court of Appeals under this provision shall not exceed six (6) months.

explanation: AMLC may inquire into/examine particular deposits/investments with banks/NBFIs notwithstanding bank-secrecy laws, through required judicial authorization and procedures, with exceptions for specified predicates/related accounts. A bank inquiry examines records; it is not a seizure. Eugenio upholds the ex parte process because advance notice could frustrate investigation.

sourceRefs.section: 8(b). Authority to inquire into bank deposits (Section 11)

verbatim: Notwithstanding the provisions of Republic Act No. 1405, as amended; Republic Act No. 6426, as amended; Republic Act No. 8791; and other laws, the AMLC may inquire into or examine any particular deposit or investment with any banking institution or non-bank financial institution

explanation: AMLC may execute or refuse (with stated reason) foreign-State assistance requests under mutuality/reciprocity; may track, freeze, restrain, seize assets, share information, and seek forfeiture; and may request foreign assistance for tracing/preservation/information. Subject to authentication, treaty, statutory, and constitutional limits.

sourceRefs.section: 8(c). Request for assistance from foreign states (Section 13)

verbatim: Where a foreign State makes a request for assistance in the investigation or prosecution of a money laundering offense, the AMLC may execute the request or refuse to execute the same and inform the foreign State of any valid reason for not executing the request or for delaying the execution thereof. The principles of mutuality and reciprocity shall, for this purpose, be at all times recognized.

explanation: Good-faith CTR/STR reporting in regular duty performance immunizes the reporter from administrative, civil, or criminal proceedings even absent prosecution. Protection covers good-faith reporting only. Citation note: syllabus cites Rule 22, Sec. 7, but the amended IRR numbers safe harbor as Sec. 6 and confidentiality of reporting as Sec. 7.

sourceRefs.section: 9. Safe Harbor Provision (2018 AMLA IRR, Rule 22)

verbatim: No administrative, criminal or civil proceedings shall lie against any person for having made a CTR or an STR in the regular performance of his duties and in good faith, whether or not such reporting results in any criminal prosecution under the AMLA or any other Philippine law.

explanation: Tiered penalties: Sec. 4(a)-(d) = 7-14 years + ≥₱3M to ≤2x value; Sec. 4(e)-(f) = 4-7 years + ₱1.5M-₱3M; last paragraph of Sec. 4 = 6 months-4 years or ₱100k-₱500k or both. Other violations (record failures, malicious reporting, confidentiality breach, knowing participation, corporate officers) and administrative sanctions separately addressed. Check the consolidated law and later amendments before applying; mind non-retroactivity.
verbatim: The penalty of imprisonment ranging from seven (7) to fourteen (14) years and a fine of not less than Three million Philippine pesos (₱3,000,000.00) but not more than twice the value of the monetary instrument or property involved in the offense, shall be imposed upon a person convicted under Section 4(a), (b), (c) and (d) of this Act. The penalty of imprisonment from four (4) to seven (7) years and a fine of not less than One million five hundred thousand pesos (₱1,500,000.00) but not more than Three million pesos (₱3,000,000.00), shall be imposed upon a person convicted under Section 4(e) and (f) of this Act. The penalty of imprisonment from six (6) months to four (4) years or a fine of not less than One hundred thousand pesos (₱100,000.00) but not more than Five hundred thousand pesos (₱500,000.00), or both, shall be imposed on a person convicted under the last paragraph of Section 4 of this Act.

explanation: Institutional definitions: AMLC (RA 9160 council), ATC (RA 9372 council), and covered institutions (same meaning as under the AMLA as amended). RA 10168 works with the AMLA's reporting/investigation/freezing/forfeiture machinery.
verbatim: (a) Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) refers to the Council created by virtue of Republic Act No. 9160, as amended, otherwise known as the ‘Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, as amended’. (b) Anti-Terrorism Council (ATC) refers to the Council created by virtue of Republic Act No. 9372, otherwise known as the ‘Human Security Act of 2007’. (c) Covered institutions refer to or shall have the same meaning as defined under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA), as amended.

explanation: Dealing covers receipt, acquisition, transacting, representing, concealing, disposing/converting, transferring/moving, use as security, and providing financial services. Designated persons span UN-designated terrorists/financiers/organizations, Human Security Act-proscribed groups, and persons whose property is seizable under that Act on probable cause.

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

verbatim: (d) Dealing, with regard to property or funds refers to receipt, acquisition, transacting, representing, concealing, disposing or converting, transferring or moving, use as security of or providing financial services. (e) Designated persons refers to: (1) any person or entity designated and/or identified as a terrorist, one who finances terrorism, or a terrorist organization or group under the applicable United Nations Security Council Resolution or by another jurisdiction or supranational jurisdiction; (2) any organization, association, or group of persons proscribed pursuant to Section 17 of the Human Security Act of 2007; or (3) any person, organization, association, or group of persons whose funds or property, based on probable cause, are subject to seizure and sequestration under Section 39 of the Human Security Act of 2007.

explanation: Property or funds span all financial assets/property plus title documents in any form (bank credits, cheques, money orders, shares, securities, bonds, drafts, letters of credit, accruing income/value). Terrorist = natural person committing/attempting/conspiring/participating/organizing/contributing to terrorist acts. Terrorist acts include statutory and treaty offenses, including civilian-targeted intimidation/compulsion violence. (Reviewer presents term names with gloss rather than a continuous quotation; no verbatim field.)

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

explanation: Financing of terrorism: direct/indirect, willful, unexcused provision/collection/possession/use of property/funds/services with unlawful willful intent or knowledge they will support a terrorist act, organization, or individual terrorist. Intent/knowledge may be proved directly or inferred; actual use of the funds is not required.

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

verbatim: Any person who, directly or indirectly, willfully and without lawful excuse, possesses, provides, collects or uses property or funds or makes available property, funds or financial service or other related services, by any means, with the unlawful and willful intention that they should be used or with the knowledge that they are to be used, in full or in part: (a) to carry out or facilitate the commission of any terrorist act; (b) by a terrorist organization, association or group; or (c) by an individual terrorist, shall be guilty of the crime of financing of terrorism.

Sec. 7: accessories profiting/concealing/assisting escape. Sec. 8: dealing with or funding designated persons' property. Sec. 9: responsible officers of juridical persons; alien deportation. explanation: AMLC (own initiative or ATC request) investigates terrorism-financing-related property/funds and probable-cause persons, enlists government assistance, and may examine deposits/investments without a court order notwithstanding bank-secrecy laws for this section.
verbatim: The AMLC, either upon its own initiative or at the request of the ATC, is hereby authorized to investigate: (a) any property or funds that are in any way related to financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism; (b) property or funds of any person or persons in relation to whom there is probable cause to believe that such person or persons are committing or attempting or conspiring to commit, or participating in or facilitating the financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism as defined herein.

explanation: AMLC (own initiative or ATC request) issues ex parte freeze-without-delay orders over related property/funds or probable-cause persons/groups/organizations, with CA extensions; targeted-sanctions freezes last until the designation basis lifts. Distinct from the AMLA Sec. 10 track where the CA issues the freeze order.
verbatim: The AMLC, either upon its own initiative or at the request of the ATC, is hereby authorized to issue an ex parte order to freeze without delay: (a) property or funds that are in any way related to financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism; or (b) property or funds of any person, group of persons, terrorist organization, or association, in relation to whom there is probable cause to believe that they are committing or attempting or conspiring to commit, or participating in or facilitating the commission of financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism as defined herein.

explanation: Sec. 12: deferral of freeze orders for investigative/prosecutorial need. Sec. 13: humanitarian withdrawals for family sustenance, counsel, and medical needs per the specified decision-maker. Sec. 19: extra-territorial reach (outward-planned/inward-directed crimes, Philippine vessels/aircraft, diplomatic premises, Filipino victims, crimes against the government; Filipino nationals abroad). (Reviewer gives operative substance, not a quotation; no verbatim field.)

Three elements of the first paragraph: issuance to apply on account or for value; knowledge of insufficient funds/credit at issuance; subsequent dishonor (including unjustified stop-payment cases). Second paragraph: failing to keep funds/credit for 90-day presentment. Corporate checks: actual signatories liable. Penalties: 30 days-1 year, fine up to double the check capped at ₱200,000, or both. Constitutional: punishes issuance of worthless checks (police power), not debt non-payment (Lozano).

sourceRefs.section: 2(a). Issuance for value — Idos v. Court of Appeals

verbatim:
SEC. 1. Checks without sufficient funds.—Any person who makes or draws and issues any check to apply on account or for value, knowing at the time of issue that he does not have sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank for the payment of such check in full upon its presentment, which check is subsequently dishonored by the drawee bank for insufficiency of funds or credit or would have been dishonored for the same reason had not the drawer, without any valid reason, ordered the bank to stop payment, shall be punished by imprisonment of not less than thirty days but not more than one (1) year or by a fine of not less than but not more than double the amount of the check which fine shall in no case exceed Two Hundred Thousand Pesos, or both such fine and imprisonment at the discretion of the court.

The same penalty shall be imposed upon any person who, having sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank when he makes or draws and issues a check, shall fail to keep sufficient funds or to maintain a credit to cover the full amount of the check if presented within a period of ninety (90) days from the date appearing thereon, for which reason it is dishonored by the drawee bank.

Where the check is drawn by a corporation, company or entity, the person or persons who actually signed the check in behalf of such drawer shall be liable under this Act.

explanation: Rebuttable prima facie presumption of knowledge when a check presented within 90 days is dishonored and the drawer, after notice of nonpayment, fails to pay or arrange full payment within 5 banking days. Dishonor alone never conclusively proves knowledge; actual receipt of written notice matters (Lim Lao; Cabrera).

Evidence of knowledge of insufficient funds.—The making, drawing and issuance of a check payment of which is refused by the drawee because of insufficient funds in or credit with such bank, when presented within ninety (90) days from the date of the check, shall be prima facie evidence of knowledge of such insufficiency of funds or credit unless such maker or drawer pays the holder thereof the amount due thereon, or makes arrangements for payment in full by the drawee of such check within five (5) banking days after receiving notice that such check has not been paid by the drawee.

explanation: Credit means an arrangement or understanding with the drawee bank for payment — not a general third-party promise to pay.

explanation: The drawee must note the dishonor reason on or attached to the check (always explicitly stating insufficient funds/credit when that is the fact, even after a stop-payment order). Sec. 3 (bank notation) is distinct from Sec. 2 (notice to drawer + 5-day opportunity).
verbatim:
SEC. 3. Duty of drawee; rules of evidence.—It shall be the duty of the drawee of any check, when refusing to pay the same to the holder thereof upon presentment, to cause to be written, printed, or stamped in plain language thereon, or attached thereto, the reason for drawee’s dishonor or refusal to pay the same: Provided, That where there are no sufficient funds in or credit with such drawee bank, such fact shall always be explicitly stated in the notice of dishonor or refusal. In all prosecutions under this Act, the introduction in evidence of any unpaid and dishonored check, having the drawee’s refusal to pay stamped or written thereon, or attached thereto, with the reason therefor as aforesaid, shall be prima facie evidence of the making or issuance of said check, and the due presentment to the drawee for payment and the dishonor thereof, and that the same was properly dishonored for the reason written, stamped or attached by the drawee on such dishonored check.

Notwithstanding receipt of an order to stop payment, the drawee shall state in the notice that there were no sufficient funds in or credit with such bank for the payment in full of such check, if such be the fact.

explanation: BP 22 prosecution is without prejudice to Revised Penal Code liability: the same check may support both a BP 22 and an estafa prosecution when each offense's distinct elements are proved (Nierras).
verbatim: SEC. 5. Liability under the Revised Penal Code.—Prosecution under this Act shall be without prejudice to any liability for violation of any provision of the Revised Penal Code.

explanation: Estafa by false pretenses/fraudulent acts, including Art. 315(2)(d): postdating a check or issuing one in payment without sufficient funds. Failure to fund within 3 days from notice of dishonor is prima facie evidence of deceit. Deceit + damage distinguish estafa from BP 22; the 3-day deceit period differs from BP 22's 5-banking-day period. Tiered penalties keyed to the fraud amount (prisión mayor minimum up to reclusion perpetua). Quotation limited to Art. 315(2), the false-pretenses forms, and the 2(d) penalty schedule.

verbatim:
ART. 315. Swindling (estafa).—Any person who shall defraud another by any of the means mentioned hereinbelow shall be punished by:

2. By means of any of the following false pretenses or fraudulent acts executed prior to or simultaneously with the commission of the fraud:

(a) By using fictitious name, or falsely pretending to possess power, influence, qualifications, property, credit, agency, business or imaginary transactions, or by means of other similar deceits.

(b) By altering the quality, fineness or weight of anything pertaining to his art or business.

(c) By pretending to have bribed any Government employee, without prejudice to the action for calumny which the offended party may deem proper to bring against the offender. In this case, the offender shall be punished by the maximum period of the penalty.

(d) By postdating a check, or issuing a check in payment of an obligation when the offender had no funds in the bank, or his funds deposited therein were not sufficient to cover the amount of the check. The failure of the drawer of the check to deposit the amount necessary to cover his check within three (3) days from receipt of notice from the bank and/or the payee or holder that said check has been dishonored for lack or insufficiency of funds shall be prima facie evidence of deceit constituting false pretense or fraudulent act.

Any person who shall defraud another by means of false pretenses or fraudulent acts as defined in paragraph 2(d) hereof shall be punished by: (1) the penalty of reclusion temporal in its maximum period, if the amount of fraud is over Four million four hundred thousand pesos (₱4,400,000) but does not exceed Eight million eight hundred thousand pesos (₱8,800,000); if the amount exceeds the latter, the penalty shall be reclusion perpetua; (2) the penalty of reclusion temporal in its minimum and medium periods, if the amount of fraud is over Two million four hundred thousand pesos (₱2,400,000) but does not exceed Four million four hundred thousand pesos (₱4,400,000); (3) the penalty of prisión mayor in its maximum period, if the amount of fraud is over One million two hundred thousand pesos (₱1,200,000) but does not exceed Two million four hundred thousand pesos (₱2,400,000); (4) the penalty of prisión mayor in its medium period, if such amount is over Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000) but does not exceed One million two hundred thousand pesos (₱1,200,000); and (5) prisión mayor in its minimum period, if such amount does not exceed Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000).

Use its definitions rather than everyday meanings. A purchase for personal, family, household or similar consumer use differs analytically from an acquisition for resale or use in production; check the statutory definition and exclusions.
Policy framework for consumer product quality and safety; starting point of the Arts. 5-16 safety/quality framework.
Deal with consumer product standards and related regulatory mechanisms, including the mandatory-standard inquiry in the exam sequence.
Address injurious, dangerous or unsafe products.
Establish special rules for new, imported and export products.
The food subchapter, separately called out by the syllabus; do not answer a food question with a generic safety rule.

The cosmetics provision, separately called out by the syllabus.
Hazardous substances, read with the statute's definitions; separately called out by the syllabus.

Prohibited acts under the quality/safety titles, separately called out by the syllabus. Where a product has been banned, recalled, misbranded or found unsafe, identify the precise legal status and the statutory actor responsible.

Deceptive sales acts and practices (described in Arts. 50-51). Identify the representation or omission, explain what impression it creates, establish materiality, and tie it to the specific prohibited category. A statement is not automatically deceptive merely because it is promotional.

explanation: Reaches conduct taking unfair advantage of a consumer's inability reasonably to protect the consumer's interests (inability to understand the transaction, ignorance, illiteracy, inability to meet essential needs, or other legally relevant vulnerability), with the circumstances specified by law. explanation: Weights and measures; a discrete article range to narrow the issue.

citation: Republic Act No. 7394, Arts. 80-94 (product-specific labeling rules)
explanation: Product-specific labeling rules (including special rules for products such as food, drugs, cosmetics, hazardous substances and cigarettes); the general minimum label is not always the whole answer.

Price-tag requirements: identify the displayed price, whether the item is covered, the rule on sale at the tagged price, and any statutory exceptions. A price tag discloses the seller's offered price; do not confuse a price-tag violation with a price-control violation under RA 7581.

citation: Republic Act No. 7394, Art. 95 (prohibited labeling/packaging acts)
explanation: Identifies prohibited label or packaging acts; the final test after establishing coverage, required label information, and category-specific rules.

citation: Republic Act No. 7394, Arts. 72-73 (prohibited warranty acts)
explanation: Identify prohibited acts involving warranties.

Cover defective products/services and common provisions. Differentiate defects in the product itself from a failure in the service provided, then identify the proper remedy and any defenses or common rules. A written warranty's duration/scope differs from the statute's separate process for defective goods/services.

citation: Republic Act No. 7581 (Price Act), Sec. 6 (price freeze)
explanation: In covered situations, such as a declared state of calamity or emergency in the relevant area, prices may be frozen at the prescribed/pre-event level for the period set by law, subject to lawful action to lift or extend the freeze. Check the exact trigger and duration from the current statute.

citation: Republic Act No. 7581 (Price Act), Secs. 7-8 (price ceiling)
explanation: A legally imposed maximum price for covered goods; distinct from the automatic/temporary freeze mechanism.
Accumulation beyond reasonable/normal inventory or in violation of the statutory standards, with the relevant intent/effect.
Sale at an excessive price or taking advantage of a shortage/abnormal situation, as defined by the statute.
Concerted practices or arrangements that manipulate supply/prices in violation of the law.

citation: Republic Act No. 7581 (Price Act), Sec. 10(4) (panic buying)

citation: Republic Act No. 10642 (Philippine Lemon Law), coverage
explanation: Strengthens protection in the purchase of a brand-new motor vehicle. Coverage: brand new, purchased in the Philippines from a covered dealer/manufacturer, and the buyer still within the statutory rights period.

citation: Republic Act No. 10642 (Philippine Lemon Law), rights period
explanation: Generally 12 months from original delivery to the consumer or 20,000 kilometres of operation, whichever occurs first. Check statutory definitions and any exclusions before applying it.

citation: Republic Act No. 10642 (Philippine Lemon Law), repair rule
explanation: The 4x-repair rule addresses repeated repair attempts for the same defect substantially affecting conformity to manufacturer specifications, value, or safe use; count attempts for the same defect, not every unrelated visit. The statute also accounts for cumulative days out of service for repair; apply the precise threshold in the current text with the facts on parts, warranty service and repair orders.

citation: Republic Act No. 10642 (Philippine Lemon Law), notice and procedure
explanation: The consumer must give the required written notice of the defect/opportunity for inspection and follow the statutory procedure; preserve dates, mileage, job orders, written notices, replies and proof of service. The statute sequences mediation, arbitration and adjudication, with remedies when the claim is meritorious or not, and rules on resale. Follow the statutory channel; do not jump to replacement/refund without testing every requirement.

Covers government branches and instrumentalities, departments, bureaus, offices and agencies, including SUCs, GOCCs, GFIs and LGUs, subject to the law's scope and any special regime/exclusion. Open, competitive procedure; the baseline modality and default starting point absent a lawful basis for a different modality.

Was evaluation performed using disclosed criteria and the legal standard? Was the ranking based on the correct measure?
Does the apparent winning bidder actually satisfy legal, technical and financial requirements?

Domestic/foreign procurement and contract price/warranty requirements; answer with the text/IRR that applies to the actual procurement.

explanation: Identify whether the respondent is a bidder/supplier/contractor or a public officer, the prohibited conduct, the governing authority, due-process step, length/scope of sanction, and appeal or reinstatement mechanism. Common requisites of pledge and mortgage: constituted to secure a principal obligation; pledgor/mortgagor must be absolute owner (subject to rules/exceptions) with free disposal or legal authority; secured obligation must be valid though future/conditional obligations may be secured as allowed; the contract does not vest ownership in the creditor; the security is accessory and generally follows/is extinguished with the obligation.

Pledge and mortgage are generally indivisible even if debt or property is divisible: the whole collateral may remain liable for the unpaid portion until full satisfaction, subject to statutory exceptions; part payment does not automatically release a proportional part absent law or agreement.

Pactum commissorium: two elements — (1) property pledged/mortgaged for a principal obligation and (2) a stipulation letting the creditor automatically appropriate the collateral on nonpayment. The automatic-appropriation stipulation is void; the security contract itself is not necessarily void in its entirety.

REM directly and immediately subjects the identified immovable and covered rights/accessions to the secured obligation; ownership stays with the mortgagor subject to the encumbrance. Art. 2124: what may be mortgaged; Art. 2125: formalities/registration (validity between parties vs. effect against third persons); Arts. 2126–2127: direct security effect and extent including improvements/accessions. Present/future obligations may be secured when intended and legally compliant, but only obligations within the mortgage's scope.

Judicial foreclosure proceeds by court action: complaint pleading mortgage and default, court determination of amount due, foreclosure judgment; the Rules govern sale, confirmation, application of proceeds, and deficiency/surplus. Equity of redemption lets the mortgagor prevent completion by paying within the allowed stage/period before confirmation of sale. Generally no post-confirmation right of redemption unless a statute (e.g., banking law) grants it.

Extrajudicial foreclosure requires a valid special power to sell plus compliance with Act No. 3135: notice, publication, place/conduct of sale, bid, and registration must be tested. The purchaser's title is subject to a statutory right of redemption where granted — typically one year from registration of the certificate of sale, subject to special rules.

Pledge requires delivery of the movable to the creditor or an agreed third person (Art. 2093); ineffective against third persons absent the required public instrument/description and Art. 2096 conditions; only movables capable of possession may be pledged; ownership stays with the pledgor. Art. 2094 limits pledging future things; Art. 2095 covers fruits/products/accessories; Art. 2097 bars pledgor alienation without pledgee consent.

The pledgee holds the collateral with a right of retention for the secured debt until obligation and charges are paid; retention is not ownership and appropriation on default is barred. The Code addresses expenses, fruits, third-party claims, return of collateral, the duty to preserve (no use contrary to law/contract), debtor/third-party-owner redemption-or-return rights, and third-party-pledgor recourse/subrogation.

On nonpayment when due, the pledgee proceeds by the Code's public auction procedure: notice, public sale, and application of proceeds. The pledgee cannot become owner automatically (Art. 2088); the statutory auction is part of the anti-pactum-commissorium safeguard.

Legal pledge: the law gives a creditor a right to retain movable property for claims related to that property or service. Syllabus examples under Arts. 1944, 1951, 1994, 2004, 546 and 1731. Method: first identify the statutory relationship (e.g., deposit, lease, repair or work), then apply the relevant retention/foreclosure rule.

citation: Chattel Mortgage Law, Act No. 1508 (form and description)
explanation: A chattel mortgage secures debt with personal property while possession generally remains with the mortgagor, under Act No. 1508 and Civil Code Arts. 2140–2141: prescribed mortgage instrument/description, affidavit of good faith, and registration for effect against third persons. Sec. 7 reasonable-description rule: the document must describe the property sufficiently to identify it; a vague catch-all may not identify specific collateral or bind third parties. The mortgagor generally must own the property or be authorized to encumber it.

citation: Chattel Mortgage Law, Act No. 1508 (foreclosure and redemption)
explanation: Chattel foreclosure follows Act No. 1508 notice/public sale procedures and application of proceeds. The syllabus distinguishes equity of redemption under the law from no right of redemption after a completed sale, subject to any special rule. In Recto Law installment sales, Art. 1484's bar on deficiency recovery after the seller elects foreclosure is critical and does not automatically extend to every ordinary loan chattel mortgage.

Reviewer pointer only: the syllabus-cited RPC Art. 319 should be checked for fraudulent/specific chattel-mortgage acts in the fact pattern. The reviewer gives no elements or text; verify the article itself before applying it.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 1-5
explanation: Title, policy, objectives, application and definitions. Sec. 4 applies to data messages and electronic documents used in commercial and noncommercial activities, including domestic and international dealings, subject to statutory exclusions and other laws. The defined terms (data message, electronic document, electronic signature, originator, addressee, information system, intermediary, service provider) are distinct and not interchangeable.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 6
explanation: Functional equivalence for writing: information is not denied legal effect, validity or enforceability solely because it is in electronic data message or electronic document form. An electronic document satisfies a writing requirement when the statutory accessibility and reliability criteria are met, centered on remaining accessible for subsequent reference with integrity safeguards.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 7
explanation: Legal recognition of electronic signatures turns on the statutory requirements: an electronic signature can identify the person and indicate approval when the applicable conditions are met. A typed name, scanned image or login is not automatically sufficient; assess reliability, intent, attribution and the relevant transaction.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 8
explanation: A retention requirement can be met electronically when the information remains accessible for later reference and the statutory conditions are satisfied, including the required form and related origin, destination and time information where applicable.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Section 9
explanation: Evidentiary weight and presumptions depend on the statute and the reliability context; authenticity of an electronic document can still be challenged.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 31-32
explanation: Confidentiality and lawful access. Separate (1) whether the record is legally recognized, (2) whether its contents are admissible and authentic, and (3) whether accessing, disclosing or using it is lawful. A valid electronic document can be unlawfully obtained, and a lawfully accessed message can still fail authentication.

citation: Republic Act No. 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), Sections 16-24
explanation: Communication of electronic documents: dispatch and receipt rules, including the designated versus non-designated information system distinction, and the statutory rules for place of dispatch and receipt and the parties' place of business. Ordinary contract formation under Civil Code Arts. 1318-1326 (definite offer, absolute acceptance, consent, object, cause) still applies; negotiation, advertisement or automated acknowledgement is not automatically acceptance.
